context.why: FairDM ships no portal roles today. An administrator has to invent them, and the three group names the framework does carry hold no permissions at all, so three places in the code grant broad rights by matching a group's name instead. This story is the foundation of the feature: it declares the four roles FairDM ships, with the exact permissions each holds, and installs them into every portal - new or already running - every time the database is brought up to date. Four later stories read what you declare here, so the shape of the declaration matters more than anything else you write.

prior_decisions: D10 - The legacy groups are renamed, not replaced. reconcile() renames Portal Administrators to Portal Administrator, Data Administrators to Data Curator and Developers to Developer, in place and only when the target name is free, because a rename carries the membership rows across and a fresh create does not. Do not delete the legacy rows and do not write a data migration.

D15 - The Portal Administrator holds no right to edit a group. Membership is edited on the Person form's groups field, so the role holds auth.view_group and contributors.change_person and nothing that can change what a role may do. Granting auth.change_group would let the role rewrite its own rights.
D17 - The module is fairdm/portal_roles.py, not fairdm/roles.py. This codebase already spends the word 'role' on contribution roles, and FR-039 exists to keep the two apart.
ARCH-001 from the design review - the declarations and the methods that read them are ONE class (PortalRoles), not a module of loose functions. Constitution Article XI.

Research R5 - the post_migrate receiver is connected with NO sender and a dispatch_uid. INSTALLED_APPS lists fairdm before the apps whose permissions the roles need, so a sender-bound receiver runs too early. Connected without a sender it runs once per app config and the last pass sees every permission, so it must tolerate a permission that does not exist yet rather than raising.

Research R1 - there are five call sites reading the legacy group names, not three. You do not remove any of them in this story; US2 does. You only make sure the Data Curator's permission list covers what they reach, including import_data and can_publish.

acceptance.given_when_then: Given the declarations module, When its four roles are read, Then they are exactly Portal Administrator, Data Curator, Community Manager and Developer; each one's permission set matches the declaration exactly rather than by subset; Developer's is empty; and the Portal Administrator's holds none of auth.add_group, auth.change_group or auth.delete_group.

Given a portal author reading fairdm/portal_roles.py, When they look for what a role holds, Then one class carries the four declarations as data plus shipped_names(), rights_carrying() and reconcile(), and every permission is written as an explicit app_label.codename.

Given an empty database, When it is brought up to date, Then all four roles exist with their rights; a second run changes nothing and duplicates nothing; permissions edited by hand are restored; the people in a role are untouched; a group the portal created itself is left alone; and a database holding the three legacy groups with members ends with those same people in the corresponding new roles.

Given any portal, When migrate runs, Then reconcile() renames the legacy rows first, then creates what is missing and sets each role's permissions, and it raises nothing when a permission it wants does not exist yet.
Given the setup pipeline, When a portal is set up for the first time, Then no groups fixture is loaded, because the file and its loaddata line are gone.
Given the contributors application, When DefaultGroups is looked for, Then it is gone; and the person filter's is_staff field no longer claims to filter Portal Administrators.

Given an administrator reading docs/portal-administration/roles.md, When they look up what a role can do, Then they find the four roles this feature ships and what each holds, and a statement that a superuser is the deployer's account while the Portal Administrator role is the portal job.
Given CONTEXT.md, When a reader looks up 'role', Then portal role, contribution role and rights-carrying role are each defined and distinguished, and the four roles are named.

Given a portal administrator upgrading to this version, When they read the changelog and the administration documentation, Then they are told that a model-level permission now applies to every instance of that model and that grants made outside these four roles should be audited before upgrading.
